Related articles Features Feb 23, 2026 The making of Claude Code View more At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. items.title: GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s
items.excerpt: GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s | vLLM Blog Menu Search Docs Documentation Blog Events Office Hours Contact Community GitHub Theme Docs Blog Events Office Hours Contact Community Search ⌘J Blog GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s October 23, 2026 13 min read vLLM Team # glm # parallelism # kv-cache # disaggregation # performance Serving long contexts in memory-constrained deployments Why not TP or DP? PCP: split the tokens, not the heads DCP: shard the KV cache too The deployment Results Making it all compose Try it Acknowledgements Notes Table of Contents TL;DR: Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP) splits each prompt across GPUs by token instead of by head, which suits GLM-5.3's sparse attention far better than tensor parallelism. Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) shards the prefill engine's KV cache by token, so a 1M context fits on the prefill node. Hybrid HiSparse lets decode keep KV in host memory, so a 1M-token request fits. On AgentX, PCP8 × DCP8 prefill with Hybrid HiSparse decode gives 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of a data-parallel deployment at the same throughput, and it is the only configuration we tested that serves 1M-token contexts. Serving long contexts in memory-constrained deployments Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. Part 1 showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ( Model Runner V2 ) makes composing all of this much easier. Why not TP or DP? items.title: Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators
items.excerpt: Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective? There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases: Verbosity bias : LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers , even when the underlying facts are wrong. Position bias : Swapping the order of two options can cause an LLM judge to flip its verdict over 75% of the time . The halo effect : Because LLMs generate text piece by piece, clean grammar and formatting can trick an AI judge into giving top marks for accuracy while missing errors. Agreeableness bias : LLM judges are great at recognizing valid work. But with detecting errors, they may fail to catch incorrect, buggy, or unsafe outputs up to 75% of the time . Self-enhancement bias: Also known as egocentric bias, AI evaluators systematically overrate outputs that were generated by themselves or from their own family. Ultimately, LLM judges are not objective arbiters of truth. They are subjective models with their own distinct biases. Treating them as infallible tools that don't need their quality measured might leave your work compromised. In this post, we’ll explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. Three helpful ways to audit your LLM judges Pillar 1: Measure internal stability Before you can trust an AI judge’s score, you need to know that it isn't just guessing. Because LLMs are probabilistic, they can be inconsistent, giving different scores to the exact same text. You can test this internal stability by running multi-pass consistency checks on a single output and calculating the variance. If a judge's scores fluctuate wildly on identical inputs, its rubric is too ambiguous. Pillar 2: Validate human alignment When your evaluation datasets are mostly valid responses, a lenient AI judge can look great on paper. It might align closely with human reviewers overall, but miss a majority of invalid or even unsafe outputs. To prove your LLM judge is catching real errors, you need chance-corrected metrics. These mathematical models filter out agreements driven purely by leniency or random chance, showing how closely your evaluator actually aligns with the informed decisions of human experts. More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025. Agent interoperability through simplicity A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. items.title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
items.excerpt: Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low-resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain-specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert-curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question-answer pairs built from real clinical-nutrition reports. Rather than a large-scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high-quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate-level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free-form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6-10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval-augmented QA as well as zero- and few-shot LLM evaluation. We report fine-tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5-fold cross-validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero- and five-shot. We further calibrate our LLM-as-judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

items.title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
items.excerpt: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.

items.title: Post-Audit Mirage: Identifiability Limits of Offline Agent Verification
items.excerpt: Offline tests can fail to reveal whether an agent update will remain safe after deployment. We operationalize this post-audit mirage using matched safe and harmful lifecycles that expose identical verifier-visible evidence while an isolated scorer records opposite deployment truth. Our theorem applies standard observational-equivalence and indistinguishability ideas to this executable audit boundary and states the resulting error-abstention tradeoff. The Post-Audit Mirage benchmark makes that boundary executable across authorization, scheduling, and shared-capacity environments. IdentifiedRangeMonitor uses fresh group-labelled harm outcomes to return deploy, hold, cannot determine, or unsupported. Experiments show that monitoring can recover the missing distinction in favorable settings but may remain undecided for rare groups, small effects, or missing observations. Verifier-agent evaluation must therefore test both calculation validity and whether the available evidence supports the deployment decision.

items.title: Adaptive Skill Granularity for Coding Agents: Runtime Routing and Macro-to-Micro Recovery
items.excerpt: Reusable skills allow large language model agents to package task-specific procedures, tool affordances, and execution guidance into modular units. Prior work has largely studied how agents retrieve, compose, or synthesize skills before execution. In coding agents, however, execution poses an additional runtime control problem: the same task may be solved through primitive tool calls, macro skills, or hybrid execution that starts with a macro and falls back to micro-level recovery. We introduce Adaptive Skill Granularity, a framework that treats skill granularity as an action-abstraction policy conditioned on task structure, execution state, and macro-skill failures. The system combines a feature-based granularity controller and a finite-state recovery executor. We evaluate the framework with a deterministic coding-agent protocol using verifier-defined success, total cost, and process metrics such as macro adoption, failure recovery, route match, and transition correctness. Results show that fixed macro execution is efficient when applicable but brittle under mismatch, while runtime routing and explicit macro-to-micro recovery improve robustness and recover controlled macro failures that fixed-granularity execution leaves unresolved. Our findings suggest that skill libraries for coding agents should be treated not only as retrievable resources, but also as controllable, verifiable, and recoverable execution abstractions.
items.notes: Runtime routing and recovery for coding agents; directly relevant.

items.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
items.excerpt: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.
items.notes: Context isolation and attention leakage; relevant to agent reliability.

items.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
items.excerpt: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.
items.notes: Long-horizon state integrity; relevant to agent memory/reliability.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language
items.excerpt: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p =0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. All artefacts are open-licensed.
items.notes: Niche low-resource adaptation; not platform/agent engineering.
